title: Making a leather apron
subtitle: Cut and assemble a full-length workshop or kitchen apron from a single section of vegetable-tanned leather with riveted straps and no sewing machine required
excerpt: How to make a leather apron from vegetable-tanned hide. Covers drafting the pattern, cutting the leather, skiving strap edges, punching holes, setting rivets, and conditioning the finished piece.
sourceNotes: Traditional leathercraft techniques as documented in public domain craft manuals. Standard harness-making and saddlery references (public domain).

glossaryTerms.definition: Leather tanned using plant-derived tannins from bark, roots, or galls rather than chromium salts. It is firm and slightly stiff when new, but moulds over time to the user and improves with wear and oil conditioning. It is the traditional choice for belts, bags, aprons, and holsters because it can be tooled, riveted, and saddle-stitched cleanly.

The process of thinning the edge or flesh side of a piece of leather with a skiving knife or edge beveller to allow the leather to fold cleanly, to reduce bulk at joins, or to taper a strap so it threads smoothly through a buckle.

A two-part metal fastener used in leathercraft: a male post and a female cap that snap together through a punched hole to permanently join two layers of leather. Available in brass, copper, and nickel. Set with a setter and anvil (or a bench vice) to prevent marking the leather face.

content.text: is hardwearing, improves with use, and can be built from a single hide section with riveted straps and no sewing machine. INTERMEDIATE: cutting leather cleanly and setting

Draw the apron body on paper or card: a full bib-front apron typically measures 550 to 600 mm across the bib and 900 to 950 mm from the top of the bib to the hem. Add a neck strap attachment point at the top corners and waist strap attachment points at the sides. Cut the paper template and test the proportions by holding against the body before cutting the leather.

Place the paper template on the leather grain side down and trace around it with a silver pen or awl. Cut along the line with the leatherwork knife, held at 90 degrees and drawn along a metal straight-edge for the long edges. Cut the neck and waist straps as separate strips, 25 to 30 mm wide. Use the upholstery shears for curved cuts at the top of the bib.
Skive and finish the strap edges
Run the edge beveller along both long edges of each strap to remove the sharp corner, which would crack under flexing.
the strap ends where they will fold through a buckle or under a rivet, thinning them to about half the leather thickness with the leatherwork knife at a shallow angle.

Punch rivet holes through both the apron body and the strap end using a leather punch or drive punch and mallet. Position the punch on a cutting mat or wooden end-grain block. Push the rivet post through from the grain side. Cap from the flesh side and set with the setter, backing the work on a steel anvil block or a bench vice. Work firmly with one clean hammer strike rather than multiple light taps.

Rub a thin coat of neatsfoot oil or leather conditioner into both surfaces of the finished apron with a cloth. Allow to absorb overnight. The oil softens the leather and improves its water resistance. Do not over-oil: too much oil darkens vegetable-tan significantly and can weaken the fibres over time.

attrs.symptom: Knife wanders from the cut line when cutting the main body
attrs.cause: The blade is not perpendicular to the leather surface, or the knife was dragged rather than drawn cleanly along a guide.
attrs.fix: Use a thick metal straight-edge clamped or held firmly. Draw the knife in one smooth pull rather than multiple short strokes.

attrs.symptom: Rivet cap is not fully set and pops loose in use
attrs.cause: The rivet setter was not squarely centred on the cap, or the setting blow was too light.
attrs.fix: Use a correctly sized rivet setter for the rivet diameter. Strike firmly and squarely. If the cap has mushroomed without setting, remove and replace the rivet.
